newsitem.title: USA: U.S. missile defense backed despite failures.
newsitem.headline: U.S. missile defense backed despite failures.

text.p: Despite four test failures, the Pentagon said on Wednesday that experts have recommended that the United States press ahead with work on a $17 billion component of its planned anti-missile defence.

The Defence Department said two independent study groups concluded that the design and concept were sound for an anti-missile missile built by Lockheed Martin Corp. for the Theatre High-Altitude Area Defence (THAAD).

"The recommendations are now under evaluation by the Ballistic Missile Defence Organisation and the Army to assess implementation" of recommendations for tight quality control in construction and testing, the Pentagon said.

The missile failed its fourth consecutive test on March 6, clouding the future of the THAAD programme and baring the technical difficulties of a "Star Wars" missile defence launched by former President Ronald Reagan.
The missile, designed to smash into attacking nuclear or other missiles at altitudes of up to 50 miles ( 80 km), failed to hit a test target at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico.
But the Pentagon said two teams found that "the THAAD design as a hit-to-kill interceptor is sound, as is the concept that THAAD will meet its operational requirements."

Senior military officials have said that failures are not unusual in early phases of such a high-tech defence system, which is also expected to include low-altitude and perhaps even space-based platforms one day.
The Clinton administration has scaled back Reagan's dream of developing a costly "Star Wars" umbrella defence of the whole United States against a massive nuclear missile attack.

But Republicans in Congress are pressing the Pentagon to expand its now-limited Ballistic Missile Defence Organisation (BMDO) plan to protect only U.S. forces and bases from missile attack until a broader threat emerges in the wake of the Cold War.

The Pentagon said on Wednesdday that two review teams appointed after the latest THAAD failure determined that the military and Lockheed Martin should move ahead with testing while assuring tight quality control in the component assembly process.

The announcemnent came one day after Lockheed Martin, Raytheon Co. and TRW Inc. announced the formation of a joint company that could one day help build Reagan's comprehensive defence against ballistic missile attack.
The three defence firms said they would each equally own the venture, to be called United Missile Defence Co., with headquarters in Crystal City, Va., near the Pentagon outside Washington.

In a joint release, they noted that each possessed unique experience in areas ranging from land- and sea-based missiles to strategic and tactical radar warning systems and battle management command and control.
